title: Chantix and Alcohol: The FDA Warning on Tolerance and Blackouts
excerpt: Can you drink on Chantix (varenicline)? What the 2015 FDA label change says about lowered alcohol tolerance, unusual behavior, and memory loss, why it happens, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Chantix? The 2015 FDA varenicline warning on lower alcohol tolerance, odd behavior and memory loss, plus practical safety tips.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Chantix (the brand name for **varenicline**, a quit-smoking pill) doesn't cause a toxic chemical reaction with alcohol the way some medicines do. But in **March 2015 the FDA changed the varenicline label** after reviewing reports that people on the drug got drunk much faster than they expected, acted in unusual or aggressive ways, or couldn't remember what happened while they were drinking. The label now tells people to cut back on alcohol until they know how varenicline affects them. Many people on Chantix have a drink without trouble, but some have a very different reaction from the one they're used to, and you can't know in advance which group you're in. Whether and how much you drink while taking it is a conversation to have with the doctor who prescribed it.

**The quick rules:** Treat your old alcohol tolerance as gone until you've learned otherwise. If you drink at all, start with far less than usual, go slowly, eat, and don't drive. Don't skip or stop doses to make room for a night out. If you or someone with you has a seizure, becomes aggressive or dangerously out of control, or has thoughts of self-harm, get help right away and call 911 in an emergency.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains the 2015 FDA safety communication, the varenicline prescribing information, and general research. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your prescriber** before drinking on varenicline if you have a history of seizures, depression, or other mental health conditions, or if you drink heavily most days. **Get medical help right away if** you have a seizure, behave in ways that are unlike you, feel agitated, depressed, or have thoughts of hurting yourself, or have swelling of the face, mouth, or throat or a serious skin reaction. In an emergency, call 911. In the US you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

## What Chantix Is and How It Works

Varenicline is a prescription drug that helps adults stop smoking. It was approved in the US in 2006 and sold by Pfizer as Chantix (Champix in many other countries). In 2021 Pfizer paused distribution and recalled brand-name Chantix in the US over an impurity found in the pills, and generic varenicline became the main version people are prescribed. The drug itself works the same way under either name, so everything in this article applies to generic varenicline too.

To understand how it interacts with alcohol, it helps to know what it does in the brain.

Nicotine works by switching on a group of receptors in the brain called **nicotinic receptors**. One type in particular (the alpha-4 beta-2 receptor) helps trigger the release of dopamine, the chemical tied to reward and motivation. That dopamine hit is a big part of why smoking feels good and why quitting is hard.

Varenicline is what's called a **partial agonist** at that receptor. In plain words, it sits in the same lock that nicotine uses and turns the key part of the way. That does two things:

1. **It takes the edge off cravings and withdrawal**, because the receptor is getting some stimulation even without a cigarette.
2. **It makes smoking less rewarding**, because varenicline is already occupying the receptor, so nicotine from a cigarette can't produce its full effect.

The usual course starts low and builds up over the first week (0.5 mg once a day, then twice a day, then 1 mg twice a day), and most people take it for 12 weeks, sometimes longer. You're usually told to set a quit date about a week after starting, so the drug is at full strength when you stop. The label says to take it after eating, with a full glass of water.

A detail that matters for alcohol: **varenicline is barely processed by the liver.** Most of it leaves the body unchanged in the urine. That's different from many medicines, where alcohol and the drug compete for the same liver enzymes. With varenicline, the interaction with alcohol doesn't seem to be about the liver at all. It appears to be about the brain.

## The 2015 FDA Label Change, Stated Plainly

On March 9, 2015, the FDA issued a Drug Safety Communication about varenicline and updated the drug's label. Here is what it said, without the softening.

**Varenicline can change the way people react to alcohol.** The FDA reviewed reports sent to its adverse event reporting system and found cases in which people taking varenicline had:

- **Decreased tolerance to alcohol.** They got drunk on less alcohol than usual.
- **Increased drunkenness.** The effects of drinking were stronger than they expected.
- **Unusual or aggressive behavior.** Some reports described people acting out of character, including aggression, while drinking.
- **Amnesia.** Some people had no memory of things that happened while they were drinking.

**The label tells patients to cut back on alcohol** until they know whether varenicline affects their tolerance. That advice is now part of the Warnings and Precautions section of the prescribing information and the patient Medication Guide.

**The same update added information about seizures.** The FDA described reports of seizures in people taking varenicline, including some people with no history of seizures, mostly within the first month of treatment. The label advises patients to stop varenicline and contact a healthcare provider right away if they have a seizure, and tells doctors to weigh the risk carefully in people with a seizure history or other factors that lower the seizure threshold.

Two things are worth being clear about. First, these findings came from reports of individual cases, not from a trial designed to measure how often the alcohol reaction happens, so no one can give you a reliable percentage. Second, the FDA kept the drug on the market and continued to say that the benefits of quitting smoking are large. The point of the label change was not "never take varenicline." It was "know that alcohol may hit you differently on it, and adjust."

### What changed later, and what didn't

You may have read that Chantix "used to have a black box warning." That's true. From 2009, varenicline carried a boxed warning (the FDA's strongest kind) about serious mental health side effects such as mood changes, agitation, and suicidal thoughts. In December 2016, after a large safety trial known as EAGLES compared varenicline, bupropion, nicotine patches, and placebo in people with and without mental health conditions, the FDA removed that boxed warning. The trial didn't find a clear increase in serious neuropsychiatric events with varenicline compared with placebo.

That later change was about mental health side effects in general. It **did not remove the alcohol warning.** The advice to cut back on alcohol until you know how varenicline affects you is still in the label. If someone tells you the Chantix warnings "went away," that's only half right.

## Why Varenicline Might Change How Alcohol Affects You

The honest answer is that the exact reason isn't established. But the biology gives a reasonable picture of why the two could interact.

**Alcohol acts on nicotinic receptors too.** Alcohol affects many systems in the brain, but part of its rewarding, mood-lifting effect runs through the same nicotinic receptors and dopamine pathways that varenicline targets. That overlap is why smoking and drinking so often go together, and it's covered in more depth in our guide to [nicotine and alcohol](/never-hungover/nicotine-and-alcohol). When a drug is sitting on those receptors and partly switching them on, it's plausible that it changes how alcohol feels and how strongly it affects you.

**It's probably not a blood-alcohol effect.** Because varenicline isn't broken down by the same liver enzymes as alcohol, there's no strong reason to think it raises your blood alcohol level by slowing alcohol's breakdown. People in the reports weren't necessarily more drunk by the numbers. They were more affected by the alcohol they had, and some behaved and remembered differently.

**Side effects can stack.** Varenicline commonly causes nausea, trouble sleeping, vivid or unusual dreams, and headaches. Alcohol causes or worsens all of those. So even setting aside the label warning, drinking on varenicline often makes the most common side effects worse, and makes the next morning harder.

**Quitting nicotine changes things on its own.** Smokers often find they feel alcohol differently after they quit. Nicotine is a stimulant, and some people use cigarettes to feel more alert while drinking. Take that away, and the sedating side of alcohol can show up more. That can make it hard to tell whether a change in how you handle drinks comes from the drug, from quitting, or from both. For safety purposes, it doesn't matter much which one it is. The result is the same: your old limits may not apply.

Interestingly, varenicline has also been studied as a possible way to help people drink less, because of that same receptor overlap. Some clinical trials have found it reduced heavy drinking in certain groups, while others found smaller or unclear effects. It isn't FDA-approved for that use, and that research is outside the scope of this article. If you're interested in it, that's a topic for a doctor.

## What This Means in Practice

The practical takeaway from the label is simple: **don't trust your usual number.** If three drinks normally leaves you tipsy but in control, three drinks on varenicline might leave you much drunker, and in rare cases might lead to behavior you wouldn't recognize as your own or a night you can't remember.

If your prescriber says some drinking is fine for you, these habits match the spirit of the label:

- **Stay within the amount your prescriber agreed**, and keep it well below your usual amount, at least until you know how you react. The label's advice is to drink less until you know how the drug affects you, not to test your limit.
- **Go slowly and eat.** Food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your blood. Varenicline is already supposed to be taken after eating, which also helps with nausea.
- **Don't drive.** The label also warns people to be careful driving or operating machinery until they know how varenicline affects them, separate from alcohol. Add alcohol and lowered tolerance, and getting behind the wheel is a bad idea even after amounts that would normally feel fine.
- **Be with people you trust.** If you have a strong reaction, it helps to have someone around who knows you're on a new medication and can notice if you're acting unlike yourself.
- **Keep your dose schedule steady.** Don't skip a dose to "make room" for drinking. Skipping doses doesn't make drinking safe and can make the quit attempt harder.
- **Pay attention to how you feel the next day.** If you have gaps in your memory, did things you regret or don't remember, or felt unusually low, anxious, or agitated, tell your prescriber. That's exactly the kind of information they need.

### Who should be especially careful

Talk to your doctor before drinking on varenicline at all if you:

- Have a history of **seizures**, or a condition or medicine that makes seizures more likely
- Have **depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or another mental health condition**
- Drink **heavily most days**, since stopping or changing your drinking can carry its own risks
- Take **other medicines that affect the brain**, such as sedatives, sleep aids, or antidepressants. Our guide to [alcohol and medications](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) covers common combinations to watch.
- Have had a **blackout** or a bad reaction to alcohol in the past

If you're comparing quit-smoking options, the other main prescription choice, bupropion (Wellbutrin or Zyban), has its own important alcohol warning centered on seizures. That's covered in our guide to [Wellbutrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/wellbutrin-and-alcohol). Nicotine replacement products like patches and gum don't carry the same kind of alcohol label warning, though drinking still tends to bring on cravings.

## Warning Signs That Need Help Now

Most people who drink a little on varenicline won't have anything dramatic happen. But know the signs that mean you or someone with you needs help:

**Call 911 or get emergency care if:**

- Someone has a **seizure**, especially one lasting more than a few minutes, or doesn't wake up normally afterward
- Someone is **so drunk they can't stay awake, can't be woken, is vomiting while barely conscious, or is breathing slowly or irregularly**. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, whatever medication is involved.
- Someone becomes **violent or dangerously out of control**
- Someone talks about **suicide or hurting themselves**. In the US, you can also call or text 988.
- There's **swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat**, trouble breathing, or a blistering or peeling rash. The varenicline label lists these allergic and skin reactions as reasons to stop the drug and get help right away.

**Contact your prescriber soon if:**

- You got drunk much faster than usual or had a memory gap after drinking
- You acted in ways that are unlike you while drinking
- You notice new or worsening mood changes, agitation, anxiety, or depression while on varenicline, whether or not you were drinking
- Nausea, sleep problems, or strange dreams are making it hard to keep taking the medicine

If your memory has gone blank after drinking, our article on [blacking out from drinking](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains what's happening in the brain and why it's a warning sign worth taking seriously.

## Drinking and Your Quit Attempt

There's another reason many doctors suggest going easy on alcohol while on varenicline, and it has nothing to do with the label warning. **Drinking is one of the most common triggers for smoking.** Alcohol lowers inhibition, a lot of people associate a drink with a cigarette, and bars and parties are where many people used to smoke. Quit-smoking programs routinely flag alcohol as a high-risk situation for slipping.

That doesn't mean you have to stop drinking to quit smoking. It means that during the first few weeks, while the habit is still fragile, it can help to:

- Drink less often and less at a time
- Have a plan for what you'll do when the urge to smoke hits
- Avoid situations where you'd usually smoke and drink together, at least for a while
- Tell friends you're quitting so they don't offer you a cigarette

Varenicline makes cigarettes less rewarding, but it doesn't erase the habit or the social pull. Keeping alcohol low gives the medication the best chance to do its job.

## Hangovers on Varenicline

Even if you don't have an unusual reaction, the morning after can be rougher than you're used to. Varenicline's most common side effects are nausea, trouble sleeping, and vivid dreams, and alcohol worsens all three. Alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night (we cover why in [can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking)), and varenicline can already disturb sleep. Put them together and you may wake up nauseated and unrested.

Some practical points:

- **Eat before you drink, and take your morning dose after breakfast** with a full glass of water, as the label directs. That helps with nausea.
- **Drink water between drinks** and before bed.
- **Don't add sleep aids** to get through a rough night without asking your pharmacist first. Combining alcohol with sedating medicines is its own risk.
- **For a headache the next morning,** check with your pharmacist about which over-the-counter pain reliever fits your situation. Our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the basics that have the best evidence.

### Where DHM fits, honestly

Some people use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven.

What matters here: **there's no research on DHM combined with varenicline**, and nothing suggests it reverses the lowered tolerance, behavior changes, or memory loss described on the Chantix label. It doesn't make drinking more on varenicline safe. If your prescriber is fine with you drinking lightly and you want to try a hangover supplement, ask your doctor or pharmacist first. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing, and our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM alongside common medicines.

The single most effective thing for a better morning on varenicline is the same as always: drink less, drink slower, and eat.

## After You Finish Varenicline

Varenicline has a half-life of about 24 hours, which means roughly half of what's in your body clears each day. Within about a week of your last dose, very little remains. There's no official waiting period before drinking after you stop.

Even so, a sensible approach is to ease back in rather than jump back to your old routine, especially if you had an unusual reaction while on the drug. And keep in mind that your tolerance may have changed for other reasons. If you drank less during treatment, your tolerance will likely be lower than it used to be, just as it would for anyone who cuts back for a few months. Our guide to [low alcohol tolerance](/never-hungover/low-alcohol-tolerance) explains why that happens.

Also, the end of a quit-smoking course is a common time to slip, and drinking is a common trigger. If you've stayed smoke-free through the course, the same caution about alcohol in risky situations still applies for a while afterward.

## The Bottom Line

- Chantix (varenicline) doesn't create a toxic chemical reaction with alcohol, but in **2015 the FDA updated its label** because some people on it had **lower alcohol tolerance, stronger drunkenness, unusual or aggressive behavior, and memory loss** while drinking.
- The label tells you to **cut back on alcohol until you know how varenicline affects you.** That warning is still in place, even though the separate boxed warning about mental health effects was removed in 2016.
- The interaction seems to happen in the brain, not the liver, which is why you can't predict it from how much you drink.
- If you drink at all, start much lower than usual, go slowly, eat, don't drive, and tell your prescriber about any unusual reaction.
- Get emergency help for a seizure, signs of alcohol poisoning, dangerous behavior, thoughts of self-harm, or a serious allergic reaction.
- Ask the doctor who prescribed varenicline what's reasonable for you. They know your health history, your other medicines, and your quit plan.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Chantix?**

Chantix (varenicline) is not one of the medicines where a single drink is known to cause a dangerous chemical reaction, but the FDA updated its label in 2015 because some people on it reported getting drunk much faster than usual, acting strangely or aggressively, or having no memory of what happened. The label advises cutting down on alcohol until you know how varenicline affects you. Whether any drinking is reasonable for you is a question for the doctor who prescribed it.

**What did the FDA say about Chantix and alcohol in 2015?**

In March 2015 the FDA issued a Drug Safety Communication and updated the varenicline label. It said the drug can change the way people react to alcohol, with reports of decreased tolerance, increased drunkenness, unusual or aggressive behavior, and memory loss for events. It also added information about rare seizures. Patients were told to decrease the amount of alcohol they drink until they know whether varenicline affects their tolerance.

**Why does Chantix make you drunk faster?**

Nobody has pinned down the exact reason. Varenicline is not broken down by the liver much, so it doesn't seem to raise blood alcohol by slowing alcohol's breakdown. The effect appears to be in the brain: varenicline acts on nicotine receptors that are also involved in how alcohol affects mood, coordination, and reward. The practical point is the same either way. Your usual number of drinks may not give you your usual result.

**Can Chantix and alcohol cause blackouts?**

Memory loss for events while drinking was one of the specific problems in the reports the FDA reviewed, and it is now described in the label. Not everyone on varenicline will have it, but it is a known risk. If you notice gaps in memory after drinking on Chantix, tell your prescriber and stop drinking while you take it until you've talked to them.

**How long after stopping Chantix can I drink normally?**

Varenicline has a half-life of about 24 hours, which means roughly half of it leaves your body each day, so most of it is gone within about a week after the last dose. There is no official waiting period for alcohol. If you had an unusual reaction to alcohol while on it, ask your doctor before assuming things are back to normal, and ease back in slowly rather than testing your old limit.

**Does alcohol make Chantix less effective?**

Alcohol doesn't stop varenicline from working chemically, but drinking is one of the most common triggers for lighting up, and the urge to smoke often rises when you drink. Many people find it easier to stick to the quit plan if they drink less or not at all during the early weeks. That is a practical point about quitting smoking, not a claim that alcohol blocks the drug.

**Is it safe to take DHM with Chantix?**

There is no research on DHM and varenicline together, so no one can say it's proven safe or unsafe. DHM does not reverse the lowered tolerance or memory problems described on the Chantix label, and it doesn't make heavier drinking safe. If you want to use any supplement while on a prescription drug, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

**Can Chantix and alcohol cause seizures?**

The 2015 label update added information about seizures reported in people taking varenicline, some of whom had no history of seizures, mostly within the first month of treatment. The FDA did not say alcohol causes these seizures, but alcohol can affect seizure risk on its own, especially heavy drinking. If you have a seizure on varenicline, stop taking it and get medical help. Call 911 for a seizure that lasts more than a few minutes or if the person doesn't wake up normally.
